newsitem.title: ITALY: Turk who shot Pope seeks Italian pardon.
newsitem.headline: Turk who shot Pope seeks Italian pardon.

text.p: The Turkish gunman who almost killed Pope John Paul in 1981, Ali Mehmet Agca, has asked Italy for a pardon from a life prison sentence or the right to move to a jail back home, his lawyer said on Monday.
Attorney Marina Magistrelli said separate requests had been submitted to Italian President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro and to the Justice Ministry 10 days ago.

She said she expected a response to take several weeks and declined to assess the prospects of success. "It is now a diplomatic issue," Magistrelli said by telephone from her office in Ancona, eastern Italy.

Agca, 38, shot and gravely wounded the Polish-born Pontiff in St Peter's Square on May 13, 1981 and was sentenced by a Rome court to a life prison term which he is serving at a jail in the town of Ascoli Piceno on the Adriatic coast.
He, his family and his lawyers used the 15th anniversary of the shooting this year to press their case for clemency, noting that the Pope had already forgiven Agca twice for the attack.
"We consider that an important factor," Magistrelli told Reuters. "The court, in passing sentence, also noted that it was being severe," she said.
Italy tried Agca for the assassination attempt under treaties regulating its relations with the Vatican.

The Holy See has made clear it does not intend to respond formally to Agca's pleas to intervene on his behalf. It has noted that recent statements by Agca, a Moslem, that he acted alone contrast with earlier assertions.

A year after the attack, Agca implicated the Bulgarian secret service and the Turkish mafia in a plot to kill the Pope on behalf of the former Soviet Union over the Pontiff's support for the Solidarity movement in his native Poland.

In March 1986 a Rome court acquitted three Bulgarians and three Turks of conspiring to kill the Pope, saying it did not have enough proof to back prosecution charges that they were in collusion with Agca.
Magistrelli said Agca had asked Scalfaro either to pardon him or commute his sentence to a lesser term.
The separate request to the Justice Ministry sought a transfer to a jail in Turkey, where he would also have to serve a 10-year sentence for the murder of a journalist.
In the submission to the ministry, Agca said he had "truly repented" for his attack on the Pope and was now "very different from the extremist student I was then".

He wrote that the shooting was "an exclusively individual act, which I carried out at a time of great political and religious excitement and when I was eager to make a hero of myself and create a sensation".
